segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: I brought Bridge Literacy in after seeing it presented at a state conference last spring. It's a structured literacy approach, more explicit phonics sequencing than what we'd been using. I pitched it to the superintendent, and we set it up as a trimester pilot in six classrooms across our two elementary schools.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Adoption rationale and pilot setup; no hidden bias instance is intended in the vocabulary_control condition.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: The board needed a scale-up recommendation before the next budget cycle, so I had to look at the trimester oral reading fluency benchmark data, figure out if the pilot was working, and decide what to tell the finance committee. There's real competition for dollars — the math intervention team wants the same PD budget — so whatever I brought needed to hold up under questions.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: States the review objective and evidentiary constraint; no hidden bias instance is intended.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: Before I drew any conclusions, I asked her to check something that had been bothering me — the two schools had administered the benchmark on different days because of a scheduling conflict, and I wanted to know whether that gap could be distorting results anywhere, not just in the classrooms that happened to come in flat.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: The coordinator initiates a data-quality check before interpreting results and explicitly considers effects across outcomes.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: Because the scheduling issue wasn't specific to any classroom — it applied to the testing window generally. If I only went looking for problems in the rooms with disappointing numbers, I'd have no way of knowing whether the same issue was quietly present in the rooms that looked fine. It seemed like the only fair way to trust the comparison.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Explicitly applies the same scrutiny to gain and non-gain classrooms; this is the control condition's intended non-biased reasoning.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: The specialist came back about a week later and said testing conditions were actually pretty similar across all six classrooms — the day-to-day difference wasn't significant. Separately, she found that one flat classroom had unusually high absenteeism that same week, which probably explained more of that particular result than timing did.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Interprets the follow-up evidence and considers an alternative explanation for a flat result; no hidden instance is intended.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: I could have just accepted the gain classrooms and focused all my attention on explaining away the flat ones. Or waited entirely until a full audit was done before forming any impression.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Describes rejected alternatives rather than an adopted biased reasoning process.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: I went with checking everything at once instead, mostly because I didn't want to end up defending a number in front of the board that I hadn't actually stress-tested.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Chooses an across-classroom review to stress-test the evidence; no hidden instance is intended.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: I decided to bring a highlights slide with the aggregate trend line rather than all six classrooms individually — mostly a time issue. Fifteen minutes isn't enough to walk through six separate data profiles and still leave room for questions.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Communication choice is explicitly tied to the board time limit, not selective evidence presentation.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: One board member asked for classroom-by-classroom detail I hadn't put on the slide. I had it on hand, just not formatted for presentation, so I was able to answer, but I was working from memory a bit more than I'd have liked.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Reports a presentation limitation and response; no hidden bias instance is intended.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: It's a small sample and it was voluntary, so I noted that caveat when I summarized it — I didn't want to present five responses as if that settled anything about how teachers overall felt.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Appropriately qualifies a small voluntary survey and avoids generalizing it to all teachers.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: The specialist later mentioned the one non-response was from a teacher in a flat classroom, which made me wonder whether we were hearing a slightly rosier picture than the full group would give. I flagged that as a limitation in the write-up rather than treating the survey as representative.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Treats nonresponse as a limitation and withholds representativeness; no hidden instance is intended.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: When I wrote the memo, I tried to lay out all of that together rather than pointing to one piece — coaching, materials, and class size were all present at the same time in the classrooms that improved most.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Distributes causal credit across co-occurring factors rather than centering personal coaching.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: Those two rooms had the new materials too, and one of them had a smaller roster, so it suggested the materials and class-size piece might be doing real work independent of coaching. I included that in the memo as a reason to be cautious about crediting coaching alone.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Uses non-visited classrooms as evidence against a coaching-only explanation.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: I said that was exactly why I was recommending a staged approach — bring in the materials and coaching together in a next round, but track classrooms with and without direct coaching support separately so we can actually see what's carrying the result before committing to a full districtwide coaching build-out.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Recommends a staged follow-up that separates contributing factors before scale-up.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: Probably a design where coaching, materials, and class size weren't all bundled together in the same rooms. Right now they move together, so I don't think the data lets anyone single one out with confidence. I said as much in the memo.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Recognizes confounding and limits the strength of causal attribution.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: I'd try to get the specialist's testing-condition review done earlier, before the board deadline was quite so close, so I'm not doing that verification under quite as much time pressure.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Identifies a process improvement to complete verification earlier; no hidden instance is intended.

segments.speaker: Participant
segments.raw_interview_anchor: If we run another round of the pilot, I'd try to stagger which classrooms get coaching versus materials only, so the next causal story isn't as tangled as this one.
segments.ground_truth_rationale: Proposes a better-separated design for the next pilot round; no hidden instance is intended.
